draft.title: Hypothetical VRAM Planning for Local LLMs: Separating Allocations
draft.body:
This post outlines a hypothetical checklist for VRAM planning when running LLMs locally. It's crucial to understand that no specific models or hardware were tested; this is purely a conceptual guide based on common allocation needs.

The core idea is to break down VRAM usage into distinct categories: model weights, KV cache, and other runtime overhead. For a hypothetical 12 GB GPU, this separation is vital for preventing Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors.

Model weights are typically the largest consumer. The KV cache size scales with context length and batch size, becoming significant for longer sequences. Other allocations include activations, optimizer states (during training/finetuning, though less relevant for inference-focused planning), and framework overhead. 

Understanding these components allows for more informed decisions about which models or configurations might fit within available VRAM. For instance, a smaller model with a large KV cache might consume more VRAM than a larger model with a small cache. This framework is intended to facilitate discussion on pre-computation VRAM budgeting.

draft.title: Conceptual VRAM Breakdown for Local LLM Inference (12GB GPU Scenario)
draft.body:
Considering a hypothetical 12 GB GPU, this guide proposes a structured approach to VRAM planning for local LLM inference. It is important to note that this is a theoretical exercise, and no actual models or hardware were evaluated.

The primary goal is to differentiate between key VRAM consumers: model weights, the Key-Value (KV) cache, and miscellaneous runtime allocations. This separation is essential for estimating feasibility and avoiding OOM errors.

Model weights represent the static parameters of the LLM. The KV cache, however, is dynamic and grows with the sequence length and batch size, significantly impacting VRAM usage during inference. Other runtime allocations can include intermediate activations and framework overhead. 

By conceptually separating these elements, users can better anticipate resource requirements. For example, a model requiring substantial KV cache due to long context windows might be unsuitable, even if its base weights are relatively small. This checklist aims to provide a framework for discussion on VRAM management strategies.
